title: The Box That Would Not Shut

title: The Quiet Seat

title: Two Pipes Under the Sink

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: Where does a community’s tap water come from, and where does used sink water go?
storyBibleReview.progression: Follow one town’s separate incoming drinking-water and outgoing wastewater routes, each with its own treatment destination.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: The sink connects two different journeys; water must be treated for its next use rather than simply disappearing.

scienceSources.title: CDC: How Water Treatment Works
scienceSources.evidence: Utilities treat source water, including river water, to remove germs and contaminants before distribution; treatment varies by source.

scienceSources.title: USGS: Wastewater Treatment Water Use
scienceSources.evidence: Wastewater includes sink water, soap and scraps; treatment reduces pollutants before environmental release and protects aquatic habitats.

title: The Bag of Wind

storyBibleReview.storySpine: Zoe wants to bring a red kite out of a low tree using a bag that stores wind, but her first gust wedges it farther in.
storyBibleReview.failedAttempt: She releases a strong gust from below the kite; the wind drives the kite deeper into the branch fork.
storyBibleReview.resolution: Zoe moves to the other side and releases a small stored puff through a narrow opening, lifting the kite toward Kit’s waiting hands.
storyBibleReview.magicRule: The separate blue zip pouch stores wind caught from a real breeze while open and sealed by its zipper. Reopening releases the stored wind in the aimed direction; a small opening gives a small puff and closing preserves what remains. It creates no new wind, and no other object is enchanted.

title: Island or Peninsula?

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a small model show the difference between an island and a peninsula?
storyBibleReview.progression: Observe water around a connected land shape, test a dry route, remove the connecting strip and compare the changed boundary.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: An island has water all around; a peninsula is almost surrounded but retains a land connection.

scienceSources.title: National Geographic Education: Peninsula
scienceSources.evidence: A peninsula is almost surrounded by water while connected to the mainland; peninsulas vary greatly in size.

scienceSources.title: National Geographic Education: Island
scienceSources.evidence: An island is land surrounded by water; islands occur in oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.

pages.pageDescription: Kit and Zoe lean over a blue tray containing a rounded clay lobe connected to clay mainland on the left.

pages.imageAlt: Zoe moves one yellow toy person along the raised clay strip from mainland toward the rounded lobe.

pages.pageDescription: A single wide lake landscape shows a small wooded island fully surrounded by water, seen from an elevated shore.

title: Marks on the Moon

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: What made the Moon’s round hollows, and why can we still see many of them?
storyBibleReview.progression: Observe a crater, follow an impact and scattered rock, then compare overlapping old/new craters and slow surface change.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Many lunar craters record impacts whose marks remain because Earth-like wind and rain do not erase them.

scienceSources.title: NASA Science: Moon Craters
scienceSources.evidence: Lunar impact craters result from colliding asteroids, meteoroids or comets; low erosion preserves many craters and ejecta.

scienceSources.title: NASA Science: Why Study Moon Craters?
scienceSources.evidence: No liquid water or wind erases lunar evidence as on Earth; impact structures preserve history.

scienceSources.title: NASA: LRO Educator Resource Kit
scienceSources.evidence: Superposition of craters reveals relative ages; impacts form different crater sizes and raised rims.

scienceSources.title: NASA ARES: Crater Comparisons student guide
scienceSources.evidence: A crater overlapping another crater’s rim must have formed later. The illustrated broken rim supplies the age clue; small size alone does not.

setting: The Moon’s gray rocky surface and black sky, moving from distant sphere to explicit illustrative close views. No people or vehicles.
props: Scattered fragments and overlapping smaller crater
coverBrief: A crisp lunar landscape shows a large bowl-shaped crater with a raised rim and a smaller crater crossing one edge, under a black sky.

pages.text: Look closely at the Moon. Many round hollows mark its surface. What punched those holes?
pages.imageBrief: Gray Moon shown large against black space with several clear circular craters and dark plains. Exact continuity: No face, cheese holes or stars visible through Moon; craters are surface depressions.
pages.imageAlt: Gray Moon shown large against black space with several clear circular craters and dark plains.
pages.pageDescription: Gray Moon shown large against black space with several clear circular craters and dark plains.
pages.state: No face, cheese holes or stars visible through Moon; craters are surface depressions.

pages.text: A rock races through space toward the Moon. The Moon has very little air to slow it down.
pages.imageBrief: One irregular gray rock approaches the lunar surface from upper left; the Moon fills lower right. Exact continuity: No flame trail or thick lunar atmosphere; illustrative distance, no scale claim.
pages.imageAlt: One irregular gray rock approaches the lunar surface from upper left; the Moon fills lower right.
pages.pageDescription: One irregular gray rock approaches the lunar surface from upper left; the Moon fills lower right.
pages.state: No flame trail or thick lunar atmosphere; illustrative distance, no scale claim.

pages.text: The rock hits hard. The crash digs into the ground and throws broken rock out around the hole.
pages.imageBrief: One impact ejects gray lunar material outward from a forming depression, viewed from a safe imaginary distance. Exact continuity: No lava eruption from below; material moves outward from strike site.
pages.imageAlt: One impact ejects gray lunar material outward from a forming depression, viewed from a safe imaginary distance.
pages.pageDescription: One impact ejects gray lunar material outward from a forming depression, viewed from a safe imaginary distance.
pages.state: No lava eruption from below; material moves outward from strike site.

pages.text: The hole is an impact crater. A raised edge, called a rim, often circles the hollow.
pages.imageBrief: Close oblique view of a simple fresh bowl-shaped crater with a clearly raised rim and scattered rock outside. Exact continuity: Impact over; no intact huge meteor sitting like a ball in crater.
pages.imageAlt: Close oblique view of a simple fresh bowl-shaped crater with a clearly raised rim and scattered rock outside.
pages.pageDescription: Close oblique view of a simple fresh bowl-shaped crater with a clearly raised rim and scattered rock outside.
pages.state: Impact over; no intact huge meteor sitting like a ball in crater.

pages.text: Some craters are small. Others are much wider than a city. Not every crash leaves the same-sized mark.
pages.imageBrief: A broad crater landscape contains one large crater and several much smaller nearby craters. Exact continuity: Natural relative crater variation; no city placed on Moon for scale.
pages.imageAlt: A broad crater landscape contains one large crater and several much smaller nearby craters.
pages.pageDescription: A broad crater landscape contains one large crater and several much smaller nearby craters.
pages.state: Natural relative crater variation; no city placed on Moon for scale.

pages.text: On Earth, rain and flowing water can wear old marks away. Wind and other changes help reshape the ground.
pages.imageBrief: An Earth hillside shows a weathered rounded crater-like basin with a small stream and ordinary clouds above. Exact continuity: Illustrative Earth comparison, green/brown ground and water; no claim about a named crater.
pages.imageAlt: An Earth hillside shows a weathered rounded crater-like basin with a small stream and ordinary clouds above.
pages.pageDescription: An Earth hillside shows a weathered rounded crater-like basin with a small stream and ordinary clouds above.
pages.state: Illustrative Earth comparison, green/brown ground and water; no claim about a named crater.

pages.text: The Moon has no rain or flowing rivers. Many crater marks remain for a very long time.
pages.imageBrief: Return to the same gray lunar crater, sharp rim dry and unchanged beneath black sky. Exact continuity: No water, clouds, grass or windblown flags; same crater as page four.
pages.imageAlt: Return to the same gray lunar crater, sharp rim dry and unchanged beneath black sky.
pages.pageDescription: Return to the same gray lunar crater, sharp rim dry and unchanged beneath black sky.
pages.state: No water, clouds, grass or windblown flags; same crater as page four.

pages.text: New impacts can change old marks. Here, a smaller crater cuts across the rim of a larger one.
pages.imageBrief: Overhead close view shows a small circular crater excavated across one section of a larger crater’s rim. Exact continuity: Small crater visibly interrupts old rim; size alone is not the age clue.
pages.imageAlt: Overhead close view shows a small circular crater excavated across one section of a larger crater’s rim.
pages.pageDescription: Overhead close view shows a small circular crater excavated across one section of a larger crater’s rim.
pages.state: Small crater visibly interrupts old rim; size alone is not the age clue.

pages.text: The broken edge is a clue. A rock hit the old crater’s rim and made the smaller crater later.
pages.imageBrief: Closer oblique angle emphasizes intact small-crater rim and the interrupted larger-crater rim on both sides. Exact continuity: Same overlapping pair; no arbitrary date labels or extra impacts.
pages.imageAlt: Closer oblique angle emphasizes intact small-crater rim and the interrupted larger-crater rim on both sides.
pages.pageDescription: Closer oblique angle emphasizes intact small-crater rim and the interrupted larger-crater rim on both sides.
pages.state: Same overlapping pair; no arbitrary date labels or extra impacts.

pages.text: Rocks hit the Moon at different times. Their craters help us work out which crashes happened first.
pages.imageBrief: Pull back to the Moon with the overlapping pair still foregrounded among many craters. Exact continuity: Full concept return; no faces, labels or unsupported ages.
pages.imageAlt: Pull back to the Moon with the overlapping pair still foregrounded among many craters.
pages.pageDescription: Pull back to the Moon with the overlapping pair still foregrounded among many craters.
pages.state: Full concept return; no faces, labels or unsupported ages.

oral.prompt: What tells us which of the two overlapping craters formed later?
oral.listenFor: The smaller crater cuts the older rim; the interrupted edge, not size alone, is evidence.

visual.prompt: Which crater breaks the edge of the other?
visual.lookFor: The smaller crater cuts through part of the larger rim.

levelRationale: App D links impact, visible landform and a supported relative-age clue. Contrast with Earth adds one explanatory relationship, while repeated concrete crater/rim language supports the ten-page progression.

title: A Trap Made of Silk

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How does an orb-weaving spider catch food without chasing it through the garden?
storyBibleReview.progression: Examine a garden orb weaver’s supported web, distinguish sticky capture lines, then follow vibration detection, prey wrapping and the small gap left by capture.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: The web is both a trap and a way to sense movement; different silk lines do different jobs.

scienceSources.title: Australian Museum: Spider facts
scienceSources.evidence: Orb webs have dry centers and spokes and sticky capture spirals; foot anatomy and limited contact help spiders move.

scienceSources.title: Australian Museum: Prey capture and feeding
scienceSources.evidence: Orb webs trap insects and spiders sense vibration; wrapping in silk subdues or packages prey.

scienceSources.title: Australian Museum: Spider webs
scienceSources.evidence: Orb web building uses frame, radii and capture spiral; species vary in web architecture.

pages.text: A fly moves through the garden. Nearby, an orb-weaving spider waits in a web shaped like a wheel.

title: One Bean Becomes Many

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can one dry bean lead to new beans?
storyBibleReview.progression: Follow a common bean seed through germination, leaf growth, flowers, pods, mature seeds and the next planting.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: The beans in mature pods are seeds that can begin another plant’s life cycle under suitable conditions.

scienceSources.title: Kew: Common bean
scienceSources.evidence: Common bean flowers produce pods containing seeds; the species has edible seeds and pods.

scienceSources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Growing beans
scienceSources.evidence: Beans germinate best in warmed soil; flowering precedes pods, and developing seeds bulge within mature pods.

scienceSources.title: Mississippi State University Extension: Beans
scienceSources.evidence: Common garden beans lift their two cotyledons above the soil during emergence; soil moisture and temperature affect germination.

scienceSources.title: West Virginia University Extension: Germinating Seeds
scienceSources.evidence: A seed contains an embryo and food reserves; root emergence and early seed-leaf support precede independent leaf growth.

scienceSources.title: Smithsonian Science Education Center: What is Photosynthesis?
scienceSources.evidence: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food. Leaves take part in the process; sunlight is energy, not a substance poured into the plant.

title: What Will the Magnet Pull?

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: Can shiny appearance tell us which objects a magnet will attract?
storyBibleReview.progression: Predict from appearance, test metal and nonmetal objects, record two groups, then test a new steel object against the revised material rule.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: Testing sorts this set by magnetic attraction; shiny appearance and the word metal alone do not predict the result.

scienceSources.title: American Chemical Society: Metals and Magnetism
scienceSources.evidence: Classroom magnets attract iron and common steel objects; aluminum foil and nonmetal items do not show the same attraction. Steel contains iron.

setting: Classroom science table in daylight. One large classroom bar magnet with fully enclosed poles; children supervised by an adult out of frame.
props: Large red-and-blue bar magnet with no printed letters
coverBrief: Kit holds a large bar magnet near a steel paper clip while Zoe compares a shiny foil ball that stays on the table; two sorting trays sit behind.

pages.text: Kit puts a shiny paper clip beside shiny foil. “Will the magnet pull both?” Zoe brings two empty trays.
pages.imageBrief: Steel clip and aluminum foil ball lie apart on the table; Kit holds large magnet and Zoe sets down two trays. Exact continuity: No loose small magnets; two test objects initially unsorted.

pages.text: The magnet pulls the steel clip. Kit lifts the magnet, and the clip hangs from one end.

pages.text: Zoe tries the foil. It stays on the table, even when the same end of the magnet comes close.

pages.text: Both objects are metal, but only the steel clip moved. Being shiny was not enough to tell them apart.

pages.text: A wooden block stays still, too. Kit puts it in the tray with the foil.

pages.text: Now Kit tries a steel washer. The magnet lifts it, just as it lifted the clip.

pages.text: Steel usually contains plenty of iron. Magnets attract iron, but they do not pull every kind of metal like this.

oral.prompt: The clip and foil are both shiny. Why are they in different trays?
oral.listenFor: Both foil and steel looked shiny, but only the steel objects were attracted by the magnet.

visual.prompt: Which shiny object did the magnet not pull?

levelRationale: App D requires revising an appearance-based prediction using several tests and applying the revised rule to a new object. The category criterion is explicit, with measured qualifications about metals.

title: Sunlight After Sunset

storyBibleReview.topicQuestion: How can a solar light shine after the Sun has set?
storyBibleReview.progression: Follow energy from daytime sunlight through a solar panel into a rechargeable battery, then to a nighttime lamp; check shade and charging limits.
storyBibleReview.synthesis: The battery makes daytime solar energy available later; the panel itself does not keep sunlight trapped inside.

scienceSources.title: U.S. Department of Energy: Solar-Powered Street and Area Lighting Considerations
scienceSources.evidence: Photovoltaic lighting systems combine a PV panel, battery and LED luminaire; solar availability and storage affect operation.

scienceSources.title: USDA Forest Service: Solar Light Towers and Mobile Solar Power
scienceSources.evidence: Solar lighting uses panels and battery storage to support night operation; stored energy has finite capacity.

setting: One ordinary garden path with a self-contained black solar path light, small square top panel, enclosed battery and white LED beneath. Day-to-night sequence. Page 8 shows only one adult hand with medium brown skin and a plain gray sleeve lifting the fallen leaf; no recurring adult character.
coverBrief: A black solar path light shines on a garden stepping stone at dusk, with its dark-blue top panel clearly visible above the lamp.

pages.text: The garden light shines after sunset. Its small solar panel is dark. What keeps the lamp glowing?
pages.imageBrief: One black solar path light casts a soft white pool on a stepping stone in evening darkness. Exact continuity: Panel unlit; no power cord or Moon beam entering it.
pages.imageAlt: One black solar path light casts a soft white pool on a stepping stone in evening darkness.
pages.pageDescription: One black solar path light casts a soft white pool on a stepping stone in evening darkness.

pages.text: Earlier, sunlight fell on the panel. The panel changed some of that light energy into electricity.
pages.imageBrief: Same lamp in bright daytime, with sunlight reaching its dark-blue square panel; LED off. Exact continuity: Explicit flashback; no stored sunlight drawn as liquid or trapped rays.
pages.imageAlt: Same lamp in bright daytime, with sunlight reaching its dark-blue square panel; LED off.
pages.pageDescription: Same lamp in bright daytime, with sunlight reaching its dark-blue square panel; LED off.
pages.state: Explicit flashback; no stored sunlight drawn as liquid or trapped rays.

pages.text: Inside the light, wires carry electricity to a battery. The battery stores energy for later.
pages.imageBrief: Simple cutaway of lamp head shows panel connected by wires to a safely enclosed rechargeable battery. Exact continuity: Technical illustration, not child opening device; continuous electrical connections.
pages.imageAlt: Simple cutaway of lamp head shows panel connected by wires to a safely enclosed rechargeable battery.
pages.pageDescription: Simple cutaway of lamp head shows panel connected by wires to a safely enclosed rechargeable battery.

pages.text: The Sun moves across the sky while the battery charges. The lamp does not need to shine in daylight.
pages.imageBrief: Afternoon view of same lamp on path, panel sunny and LED off; shrub shadow falls away from panel. Exact continuity: Single moment; no multiple suns; battery remains inside.
pages.imageAlt: Afternoon view of same lamp on path, panel sunny and LED off; shrub shadow falls away from panel.
pages.pageDescription: Afternoon view of same lamp on path, panel sunny and LED off; shrub shadow falls away from panel.
pages.state: Single moment; no multiple suns; battery remains inside.

pages.text: As evening grows dark, a control switches the lamp on. The battery now supplies energy to the light.
pages.imageBrief: At dusk, same lamp begins glowing while the panel lies in dim light. Exact continuity: Automatic control is internal; no child switching exposed wires.
pages.imageAlt: At dusk, same lamp begins glowing while the panel lies in dim light.
pages.pageDescription: At dusk, same lamp begins glowing while the panel lies in dim light.
pages.state: Automatic control is internal; no child switching exposed wires.

pages.text: That is why the lamp can glow without sunlight. Energy collected earlier is being used now.
pages.imageBrief: Nighttime cutaway shows the enclosed battery connected to the lit LED beneath the dark panel. Exact continuity: No arrows needed; electrical route visible; panel not producing at night.

pages.pageDescription: Nighttime cutaway shows the enclosed battery connected to the lit LED beneath the dark panel.

pages.text: The battery stores only some energy. If little sunlight reaches the panel, the lamp may shine for a shorter time.
pages.imageBrief: A daylight view of the same garden light shows the shrub’s shadow covering most of its top panel while the surrounding path is sunlit. Exact continuity: One daytime cause of weak charging; lamp off in daylight; no nighttime shadow falsely shown as blocked sunlight.

pages.pageDescription: A daylight view of the same garden light shows the shrub’s shadow covering most of its top panel while the surrounding path is sunlit.

pages.text: A leaf covers part of this panel during the day. Removing it lets more sunlight reach the panel again.
pages.imageBrief: Daytime close view shows one adult hand lifting a fallen leaf from the solar panel. Exact continuity: Time transition clear; leaf removed, no electrical disassembly.
pages.imageAlt: Daytime close view shows one adult hand lifting a fallen leaf from the solar panel.
pages.pageDescription: Daytime close view shows one adult hand lifting a fallen leaf from the solar panel.

pages.text: People make the lamp and battery from materials such as metal and plastic. Switching the lamp off saves stored energy.

pages.text: The battery stores energy during the day. At night, that energy powers the lamp and lights the garden path.
pages.imageBrief: Final evening view shows the same lamp lighting the next stepping stone, with clear path and quiet garden beyond. Exact continuity: Same device, no additional lamps; endpoint resolves opening nighttime glow.

oral.prompt: Which part lets the light use daytime energy after sunset?
oral.listenFor: The rechargeable battery stores energy; the solar panel converts light but does not store it itself.

visual.prompt: What connects the battery to the glowing lamp?
visual.lookFor: The enclosed wires complete the route to the LED.

levelRationale: App D tracks a three-part energy system across a flashback and evening return. Concrete parts and explicit time markers support the distinction between converting energy and storing it.
